title: Performance Mindset & Measurement
summary: The discipline behind every optimization: measure first, name your bottleneck, and know what you're actually trading. Covers latency vs throughput, Amdahl's Law, and the two pitfalls that waste the most engineering time.

slides.markdown:
"The site feels slow" is not a bug report an engineer can act on. Performance engineering starts by turning that feeling into a number: which request, what percentile, how many milliseconds, measured where.

The discipline in this topic is the one that separates engineers who fix the real bottleneck from ones who guess and tune whatever looks suspicious. It rests on four ideas: measure before you touch anything, know which metric you're actually optimizing, understand the ceiling a serial bottleneck imposes on you, and set a target before you start so you know when to stop.

Get this mindset wrong and every later topic in this group — profiling, benchmarking, latency work — gets pointed at the wrong target.

slides.subTitle: Intuition about bottlenecks is usually wrong
slides.markdown:
Ask an engineer where their service spends its time and you'll get a confident answer — usually wrong. Studies of real profiling sessions repeatedly find the actual hot spot is somewhere the engineer wasn't looking: a logging call that serializes a large object, a regex compiled on every request, a connection pool that blocks.

Intuition fails because modern systems hide cost. A one-line function call can hide a network round trip, a lock acquisition, or an O(n²) loop behind an innocent-looking name. You cannot eyeball your way to the truth of a system you didn't write every line of, and often can't even for one you did.

The fix is procedural, not talent-based: **profile before you optimize, every time**, even when you're sure you already know the answer. Treat your own certainty about the bottleneck as a hypothesis to test, not a fact to act on.

slides.subTitle: Optimizing one can hurt the other
slides.markdown:
**Latency** is how long one request takes. **Throughput** is how many requests the system completes per unit time. They sound like two views of the same thing, but they trade against each other constantly.

Batching is the clearest example: grouping 100 writes into one disk flush multiplies throughput, because the fixed cost of a flush is amortized across all 100. But the first write in that batch now waits for the other 99 to arrive — its latency went up. A database that fsyncs every 10ms instead of every write trades individual write latency for total write throughput.

The reverse trade shows up too: adding more worker threads can raise throughput up to a point, then context-switch overhead and contention start eating into it, and both metrics get worse together — the sign you've crossed into over-parallelization, covered in this group's concurrency topic.

The practical rule: before optimizing, say out loud which metric you're improving and confirm it's the one the business actually cares about. A batch job cares about throughput; a checkout API cares about latency, specifically the tail.

slides.subTitle: The speedup ceiling imposed by the part you didn't optimize
slides.markdown:
Amdahl's Law puts a hard number on a common mistake: optimizing a part of the system that was never the constraint. If a fraction **P** of the total time is parallelizable (or speedable-up) and the rest, **(1 − P)**, is not, the maximum possible speedup — even with infinite resources thrown at P — is:

**speedup ≤ 1 / (1 − P)**

Concretely: if 80% of a request's time is spent in a step you can parallelize perfectly and 20% is serial (auth check, response serialization, whatever can't be split), the *ceiling* on total speedup is 1 / 0.2 = **5x** — no matter how many cores you throw at the 80%. Go from 4 cores to 4,000 cores on that portion and you still cap out around 5x overall.

The practical use isn't the formula — it's the instinct it builds: before scaling up a fix, ask what fraction of total time it actually touches. Engineers routinely 10x a hot loop that was 15% of total latency and are confused when overall latency barely moves. Amdahl's Law says exactly why: the other 85% is now the ceiling.

slides.subTitle: A request's time budget
slides.markdown:
Take a single API request and break its total latency into the parts that actually consumed time: DNS/TLS handshake, load balancer queueing, application code, a database query, a downstream service call, response serialization, network transfer back to the client. Line them up as stacked segments summing to the total.

The point of drawing this out is that in most real systems, one or two segments dominate and the rest are noise — but which ones dominate is almost never obvious without measuring, and it differs request to request. A request that's slow because of a cold database connection looks identical from the outside to one that's slow because of a large response payload; only the breakdown tells them apart.

This is also the diagram to hand a teammate who says "the API is slow" — ask them which segment, because "the API" isn't a single thing you can optimize.

slides.subTitle: The biggest single win beats broad micro-tuning
slides.markdown:
A system's overall speed is set by its slowest constrained resource — the bottleneck — and improving anything else does close to nothing. This is the operational consequence of Amdahl's Law: find the segment that dominates the time budget (§5) and attack that one first.

The common failure mode is **broad micro-tuning**: shaving 5% off ten different functions because they're the ones you understand best, while the one function that's 60% of the total sits untouched because it looked scary or belonged to another team. Ten 5% wins on non-bottlenecks move overall latency by roughly nothing; one 20% win on the actual bottleneck moves it by close to 20%.

The practical loop is: measure, identify the single largest contributor, fix only that, re-measure. Repeat. This is slower to start than tuning everywhere at once, but it's the only loop that guarantees each round of work produces a visible result — and a visible result is what tells you whether to keep going or move to the next constraint.

slides.sectionTitle: Set the budget before you optimize
slides.markdown:
A performance budget is a target set **before** work starts, not discovered after the fact by seeing how fast you can go. "Checkout API p99 under 300ms" is a budget; "make checkout faster" is not — it has no stopping condition.

Budgets do two jobs. First, they tell you when to stop: without one, optimization tends to continue past the point of diminishing returns, burning engineering time for improvements users can't perceive (below roughly 100ms, most people can't distinguish further gains). Second, a budget forces you to name the metric and the percentile up front (§3, and the tail-latency discussion in this group's Latency Optimization topic), which prevents the common failure of celebrating a p50 win while p99 got worse.

Good budgets are also allocated per component, the same way a financial budget is: if the whole request must stay under 300ms and the network round trip is a fixed 40ms, the remaining 260ms gets divided among app code, database, and downstream calls — so a team doesn't optimize a piece that was never going to blow the budget while ignoring the one that will.

slides.subTitle: Rough orders of magnitude
slides.markdown:
Good performance judgment leans on a handful of memorized orders of magnitude — you don't need exact figures, just which bucket an operation falls into:

- **L1 cache reference:** ~1 ns
- **Main memory reference:** ~100 ns
- **Same-datacenter network round trip:** ~0.5 ms
- **SSD random read:** ~100 μs–1 ms
- **Cross-region network round trip:** ~50–150 ms
- **Rotational disk seek:** ~5–10 ms

The gaps between these are the whole point: a main-memory access is ~100x an L1 hit, and a cross-region call is roughly 100,000x a same-datacenter one. These ratios explain why "just add a network call" inside a hot loop is a much bigger sin than an extra memory allocation, and why moving a single blocking cross-region call out of a request path can outweigh weeks of in-process micro-tuning.

You don't need to recall these to two significant figures in an interview — you need the *relative* gaps, so you can immediately rank candidate bottlenecks without a profiler.

slides.subTitle: Tuning code that was never the bottleneck
slides.markdown:
Donald Knuth's full quote is sharper than the fragment everyone repeats: "premature optimization is the root of all evil... yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical 3%." The point isn't that optimization is bad — it's that optimizing **before you know where the 3% is** wastes effort and, worse, actively harms the codebase.

The cost isn't just wasted time. Premature optimization typically means: hand-inlining functions that made the code harder to read, adding a cache with its own invalidation bugs, or choosing a more complex data structure — all to speed up code that turns out to be 0.5% of total runtime, while making the code measurably harder to maintain for everyone after you.

The fix is ordering, not restraint: write clear code first, profile under realistic load, and only optimize the segment that measurement identifies as significant. "Should I optimize this?" is answered by a profiler, never by a hunch about which function looks slow.

slides.subTitle: A benchmark that doesn't represent production
slides.markdown:
A benchmark that doesn't look like production traffic tells you the truth about a system nobody runs. Common ways this goes wrong: benchmarking with all-cache-hit requests when production sees 30% cache misses, using uniformly-sized payloads when real traffic is heavy-tailed, or running single-threaded when production always has concurrent load contending for the same locks and connection pool.

The result is an optimization that measurably wins on the benchmark and does nothing — or actively regresses — in production, because the benchmark never exercised the path production actually takes. A cache-focused optimization tested only against cache hits looks free; deployed against real traffic with real misses, its added bookkeeping shows up as pure overhead.

This is fixed the same way as bottleneck-finding: measure the *real* traffic shape (request size distribution, cache hit rate, concurrency level, error rate) before designing the benchmark, and treat a benchmark's result as provisional until it's validated against production numbers or a shadow/replay test (covered in Benchmarking Methodology and Capacity Planning & Load Testing).

A complete performance mindset, stated as a loop: set a budget for the metric that matters (§7), measure the real system under realistic load rather than guessing (§2, §10), find the single dominant contributor (§5, §6), understand the ceiling the untouched parts impose on any fix (§4), and stop once the budget is met rather than continuing to chase diminishing returns.

Every later topic in this group is a tool for one step of that loop: profiling techniques and benchmarking methodology are how you measure, algorithmic and latency optimization are what you do once you've found the bottleneck, and capacity planning is how you validate the fix under real load. None of them are useful without this loop wrapped around them — a perfect profiler pointed at the wrong question just produces a very precise wrong answer.

The senior-level tell in this area isn't knowing more optimization tricks; it's refusing to apply any of them until measurement says where they belong.
